title: Permissions in a billing tool
excerpt: Show a finance lead what they can issue, void, or only draft, and why a control is locked. Hidden buttons feel like bugs on a money screen.
alt: A white wall covered with framed prints, small plants, and two floating shelves, objects left in view instead of stored out of sight.
caption: A wall of prints and shelves, the arrangement left visible. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Should send be hidden if someone can only draft?
faqs.answer: Show Send as unavailable and say why, for example that they can draft and a second person has to send. A finance lead who cannot see the control will assume the product is broken or will find a path around it. Hiding the lock makes the rule look like a bug.

faqs.question: Who should be able to void an invoice?
faqs.answer: Fewer people than can draft one. Void is a ledger event. The people who may do it should see a confirmation that names the invoice, the amount, and the recipient. Everyone else should see Void explained, not absent, unless your policy truly forbids them from knowing the action exists.

faqs.question: What about bank details and tax settings?
faqs.answer: Bank details and tax settings are not everyday invoice permissions, so keep them in a tighter role. Tell the lead that bank details are visible to the owner without putting the full account number on the draft they are checking. Explain the boundary in one sentence rather than with a generic forbidden page.

markdown:
Billing tool permissions UX should show the finance lead what they can do, and why a control is unavailable. The person who is afraid of a wrong invoice will read a missing Send button as a defect. They will refresh, they will try another browser, and they will ask a colleague to log in and look. Show the button. Say who is allowed to press it.

A hidden money control is folklore waiting to start.

## Draft, send, void

Separate the verbs before you design the locks. Drafting is preparing a number. Sending is telling a customer. Voiding is undoing a tell. Those are different risks, and a single role called "finance" that can do all three is how a nervous afternoon becomes a voided invoice that was actually correct.

A common, sane split: many people can draft, fewer can send, fewer still can void or refund. Write the split in the interface, on the invoice, in the lead's words. "You can edit this draft. Sending needs a second approval from Jordan." That sentence prevents the lead from hunting for a bug, and it prevents Jordan from being surprised by a ping with no context. The approval should show the same amount, recipient, and tax the drafter saw. Approval of a summary that hides the lines is how the second person rubber-stamps the wrong invoice. Put the fear in front of the approver too.

Do not invent a fourth verb, "submit for review," unless it is truly different from draft. Extra verbs are extra ways to think something was sent. If the status is still draft, say draft, even while it is waiting on Jordan. "In review" is acceptable if you define it as not sent. Define it on the screen, not in a wiki.

[The WCAG 2 overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) describes perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust interfaces, including web applications. A permission that exists only as a missing control is not perceivable. A disabled control with a text reason is. Do not rely on a lock icon alone, or on a color. The sentence has to travel with the control into a screen reader and into a screenshot the lead pastes in a chat. "You can't" with no reason will come back to you as a ticket. The reason is the product.

## What the lead can see

Visibility is its own permission. Seeing an invoice, seeing the customer's email, seeing a bank account, seeing a full card number, seeing another entity's books: decide each one. The lead who is trying not to send a wrong invoice usually needs the amount, the lines, the tax, the recipient email, and the status. They often do not need the full payout account number on that same screen. Mask it, and say "Payout account ends in 4412, visible to the owner." The mask is not a puzzle. It is a boundary they can repeat to an auditor.

If they cannot see an invoice at all, search and lists should not pretend it does not exist when they are trying to reconcile a number a customer mentioned. "An invoice exists for this amount. You do not have access" is awkward and sometimes necessary. Silence looks like a missing payment. On a finance tool, a missing payment starts a process. Do not start that process with a white lie in the empty state.

[Google's people-first guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) puts extra emphasis on trust for topics that can affect financial stability. Permissions are a trust feature. A role matrix in a settings page that nobody can explain is not. The invoice screen is where trust is checked, every send. Write the role in language an owner can audit without a diagram. If you cannot say the rule in a sentence, the rule is not ready to enforce on a person.

## Second approval without a maze

Approval should be a single screen with the facts and two verbs: send, or return with a note. The note is required on a return, and it should land on the draft where the drafter will see it, next to the lines, not in an inbox they check later. "Tax looks off on the second line" is the kind of note that prevents the wrong send. A bare rejection with no note creates a resend of the same invoice, which is the fear, delayed by a day.

Do not make the approver recreate the invoice in their head from a chat message. The notification can be short. The destination of the notification must be the invoice. Deep-link there. If the link opens the dashboard, the approval will happen from memory, and memory is how digits swap.

When the approver is unavailable, the product needs a visible fallback, not a shared password. "Jordan is out. Sam can send until Friday" is a temporary permission with an end. Show the end on the invoice. When Friday passes, the button returns to its explanation. Silent expiration is the Monday bug report. Say the date while the exception is live.

Escalation is a sentence, not a new product area. If no approver is configured, block send and say "No one is set to approve sends. Add an approver in settings." Do not fail at click-time with a generic error after the lead has already promised a customer the invoice is on its way. The block should be visible while they are still drafting, as soon as the invoice is complete enough to be dangerous.

## Locked, not hidden

On the draft, Send can be disabled with the reason beside it. Void, if they cannot void, can be disabled with "Only the owner can void a sent invoice." Refunds, same pattern. The lead learns the shape of the ledger from the disabled verbs. A screen that only shows the verbs they have looks simpler in a usability test with one role, and collapses the moment two roles share a desk.

Hide a control only when knowledge of it is itself the leak. A control that issues a manual payout to a bank account might be one of those, for a clerk who should not know manual payouts exist. Be stingy with this exception. Invoice send is not one of them. Everyone in finance knows sending exists. Hiding it insults them and creates the bug report.

The server still enforces the rule. A disabled button that the API accepts is a costume, and costumes do not belong near money. Test with the network tab, or with a second client, if that is how your team verifies. The design is not done when the pixels are gray. It is done when the forbidden action does not happen and the allowed action does.

Old links and stale tabs deserve the same sentence. They approve on a tab that was open before you removed their right. The action fails, the draft remains, and the text explains the new boundary. It does not show a stack trace, and it does not succeed because the tab was born in a more privileged minute.

## A second seat in the test

Test with two accounts: a drafter and a sender. The drafter prepares an invoice with an obvious oddity, a round number that should have tax. They should see, without help, that they cannot send, and who can. The sender opens the same invoice and should see the lines, not a summary card. They send, or they return it. Then the drafter's screen updates without a reload scavenger hunt. Status moves from draft to sent, or the note appears. If either person calls the other to ask what the button did, the permission UI failed, even if the ledger is correct.

Repeat the test for void, for a refund, and for viewing a masked bank detail. Three tests. They will not all pass the first time, because teams design the send path and improvise the rest. Improvisation is where hidden buttons return.

Include a screen reader pass on the disabled send button. The name, the state, and the reason should be one announcement. "Send, unavailable, needs a second approval from Jordan" is the announcement you want. "Button, dimmed" is not an announcement. It is a prop.

## Do not encode panic into the default role

The temptation after a real wrong invoice is to remove send from everyone and add a heavy approval on every correction, including a typo in a memo. Design the lock to match the risk. Sending and voiding stay gated. Editing an internal note does not need a committee. If every field requires approval, people will batch work outside the tool, in a spreadsheet, and paste the result in a hurry. The hurry is the new risk. You will have built a permission system that pushes the dangerous moment offstage, where you cannot see it.

Review the roles twice a year, or after any incident, with the sentences still on the invoice. If the sentences have become "ask someone," the roles drifted into folklore again. Tighten the copy until a new lead can explain the boundary on their first afternoon.

The place they look when the invoice is not on the list is search, and search has to respect the same sentences. [Search inside a billing tool](/blog/search-inside-a-billing-tool) is the next piece, because a lead searches when the status filters fail, and the matches have to use the words draft, sent, paid, and void, with a way back to the invoice they left.
